headline: Massachusetts takes on larger SNAP administration bill as federal share drops
dek: A federal law cuts Washington's share of state SNAP operating costs from 50% to 25%, adding an estimated $53 million to Massachusetts' current-year burden as eligibility work and call-center demand remain under pressure.
body: Massachusetts is beginning a new federal fiscal year with a larger bill for running the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, after a federal law reduced Washington's share of state administrative costs from 50% to 25%. The change affects the machinery behind SNAP — including eligibility processing, benefit issuance and related systems — rather than directly removing the federal dollars loaded onto households' electronic benefit cards. WBUR reported that the shift requires Massachusetts to absorb an estimated additional $53 million during the current fiscal year.

The change comes from Section 10106 of Public Law 119-21, the reconciliation law enacted in July 2025. The U.S. Government Publishing Office's text says the federal government will cover 50% of eligible state administrative costs through fiscal year 2026, then 25% beginning in fiscal year 2027. Because the federal fiscal year began Oct. 1, 2026, the lower reimbursement rate is now in effect. The law is available at https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-119publ21/html/PLAW-119publ21.htm.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food and Nutrition Administration described the same change in a June proposed rule. The agency said the rule would update SNAP regulations to match the law, while leaving the categories of allowable administrative expenses and the basic reimbursement procedures in place. The proposal is at https://www.fna.usda.gov/snap/fr-062426. That distinction matters: the statute has changed the funding split, while USDA's rulemaking is the regulatory step explaining how the change fits into existing program rules.

For Massachusetts, the new expense arrives while the agency that administers SNAP is already under strain. WBUR reported that federal data showed enrollment in the state had fallen by nearly 190,000 after the 2025 law added eligibility requirements. The report also said the Department of Transitional Assistance faces a lawsuit alleging that roughly 80% of SNAP-related calls have been dropped. Those are reported conditions and allegations, not a finding that every missed call or enrollment change was caused by the cost-sharing provision.

The operating-cost change is separate from the annual adjustment to household benefits. Massachusetts' Department of Transitional Assistance says the maximum monthly allotment for one person rose from $291 to $292 effective Oct. 1, while the maximum for a four-person household rose from $973 to $975. The agency cautions that most households do not receive the maximum; income, shelter, utility, child-care and certain medical deductions affect the individual calculation. Its table is available at https://www.mass.gov/info-details/snap-cost-of-living-adjustments-cola.

That separation helps explain why families may see a small benefit increase even as the state faces higher administrative costs. The federal government continues to finance the underlying SNAP allotments, but Massachusetts must find more state money for the workers, technology and customer service needed to determine eligibility and deliver those benefits. Food-assistance organizations told WBUR the cost shift adds pressure at a time when the department is understaffed.

The law also sets up a possible second financial exposure. Starting in a later fiscal year, states can be required to share part of the cost of SNAP benefits based on payment-error rates. WBUR cited a Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimate that Massachusetts could face as much as $350 million in additional costs under that provision, but that figure is an outside estimate rather than a current bill or a final federal assessment. The timing and amount would depend on the rules and the state's measured error rate.

The immediate question for Massachusetts is how the administration and Legislature will cover the $53 million administrative gap without slowing applications, renewals or case assistance. People receiving SNAP can check their current balance and notices through DTA Connect or the phone number on the back of their EBT card, while advocates and food banks are watching whether the added state obligation shows up as longer waits or more demand for emergency groceries. The federal cost shift is settled; its effect on service quality will become clearer as the state operates under the new funding formula.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Massachusetts SNAP administration costs rise in 2026
seoDescription: Massachusetts must absorb an estimated $53 million more in SNAP administrative costs after the federal reimbursement share fell from 50% to 25%.
